raw_case_text:
On June 14, 2024, an otherwise healthy 50-year-old male former military service member sought care at a primary care center in Bogota (capital city of Colombia) after 7 days of fever (up to 39 C), chills, diaphoresis, myalgias, arthralgias, and headache. He reported a 2-day history of epigastric pain, loose stools, and dark urine. His illness was considered an unspecific viral infection, and he was discharged. His signs/symptoms had begun 10 days after he returned from Grande Comore Island, where he had stayed for 2 weeks while providing military training. Until his travel to the Comoros, he had not been in another P. vivax/P. falciparum-endemic area in the previous 5 years. On June 15, 2024, he was admitted to Hospital Militar Central, a reference military hospital in Bogota, for a syncopal episode, disorientation, and jaundice. Physical examination revealed hypothermia, tachycardia with Kussmaul breathing, and reduced oxygen saturation. The patient was jaundiced and stuporous with no bleeding.
Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, malarial hepatopathy, renal impairment, metabolic acidosis, and hyperlactatemia (Table). Thick and thin blood smears showed P. falciparum (17,840 trophozoites/muL; parasitemia of 0.35%) with gametocytes and P. vivax (8,320 trophozoites/muL). Severe malaria was diagnosed, and treatment with intravenous artesunate was initiated (2.4 mg/kg) in addition to fluid resuscitation and invasive mechanical ventilation support. However, the patient experienced 2 episodes of cardiopulmonary arrest and died. Autopsy and histopathologic examination of heart and brain samples revealed multiple parasitic structures compatible with Plasmodium trophozoites (Appendix Figures 1, 2). PCR performed on blood smears confirmed the presence of P. falciparum and P. vivax (Appendix). DNA gene fragments from the small subunit rRNA 18S gene were sequenced from the positive specimens, and phylogenetic analyses positioned the obtained sequences in the same subclade as P. falciparum sequences detected in South Africa and as P. vivax sequences detected in Cameroon, Nigeria, China, and India (Figure; Appendix). Sequences were deposited in GenBank (P. falciparum accession no. PQ408861, P. vivax accession no. PQ408862).
In the most recent study that used PCR to assess the distribution of Plasmodium spp. on Grande Comore Island, among 159 positive samples collected during 2012-2013, nearly all (98.11%) were positive for P. falciparum and only 1.25% were positive for P. vivax. At that time, the authors indicated that routinely, without PCR testing, the rapid diagnostic tests used in the Comoros were able to identify P. falciparum but no other Plasmodium spp., which is in accordance with a recent published editorial that discusses the contemporary concern with regard to the need to re-evaluate the spread of P. vivax in sub-Saharan Africa. The editorial mentioned that during 2017-2021, among 1.57 billion malaria rapid diagnostic tests purchased for use by sub-Saharan Africa national malaria control programs, 79.4% were focused on identifying P. falciparum and the remainder were combination tests lacking P. vivax specificity; thus, the predominant approach for malaria diagnosis across Africa was unable to specifically detect P. vivax. Our report highlights the value of strengthening laboratory diagnostic tools with good performance for detecting and accurately identifying Plasmodium spp. in clinical settings and of conducting more genetic-epidemiologic studies in the Comoros and other sub-Saharan Africa countries.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male former military service member presented with a 7-day history of high fever, chills, diaphoresis, myalgias, arthralgias, and headache, followed by epigastric pain, loose stools, dark urine, syncope, disorientation, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days after returning to Bogota, Colombia, from a 2-week military training stay on Grande Comore Island, the patient developed 7 days of fever (up to 39 C), chills, diaphoresis, myalgias, arthralgias, and headache, plus 2 days of epigastric pain, loose stools, and dark urine. Initially discharged from primary care with a diagnosis of nonspecific viral infection, he was admitted the next day (June 15, 2024) after a syncopal episode, disorientation, and jaundice.
subjective.past_medical_history: Otherwise healthy former military service member; traveled to Grande Comore Island (Comoros) for 2 weeks; no other travel to P. vivax/P. falciparum-endemic areas in the prior 5 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, diaphoresis, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, epigastric pain, loose stools, dark urine, syncope, disorientation, and jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: Hypothermic, tachycardic, with Kussmaul breathing, reduced oxygen saturation, jaundice, and stupor, without clinical bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs demonstrated leukocytosis, anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, malarial hepatopathy, renal impairment, metabolic acidosis, and hyperlactatemia.
objective.advanced_workup: Postmortem autopsy and histopathological examination of heart and brain tissues demonstrated multiple intra-vascular parasitic structures compatible with Plasmodium trophozoites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal severe mixed Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax malaria imported from Grande Comore Island. Confirmed by thick and thin blood smears showing P. falciparum (17,840 trophozoites/uL; 0.35% parasitemia with gametocytes) and P. vivax (8,320 trophozoites/uL), as well as 18S rRNA PCR and phylogenetic sequencing (GenBank PQ408861 and PQ408862). Treated with IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg), fluid resuscitation, and invasive mechanical ventilation, but suffered two cardiopulmonary arrests and died.
